content: Actinic keratosis is a small, rough, raised lesion that typically develops on areas of the skin exposed to the sun over an extended period. Over time, some actinic keratoses may progress into a type of skin cancer. Symptoms of Actinic Keratosis: Actinic keratosis commonly appears on sun-exposed areas such as the face, scalp, back of the hands, chest, or other regions frequently exposed to sunlight. These lesions may vary in color, appearing gray, pink, red, or matching the surrounding skin tone. Often, they are covered with a white or yellowish scale. Initially, the lesions present as flat, scaly patches. Over time, they may become hard, wart-like, or develop a gritty, rough, sandpaper-like texture. In some cases, the surface may take on a horn-like appearance. These lesions are often easier to feel than to see. Causes of Actinic Keratosis: The primary cause of actinic keratosis is prolonged exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun. However, it typically takes many years or even decades for these lesions to develop. Risk Factors: Certain factors increase the likelihood of developing actinic keratosis, including: Having fair skin, blue or green eyes, or blond or red hair. A history of kidney or other solid organ transplants, particularly in individuals taking immunosuppressive medications. Long-term, daily sun exposure, such as in outdoor occupations. Experiencing multiple severe sunburns during childhood or early life. Older age. Diagnosis: A healthcare provider can diagnose actinic keratosis based on the appearance of the skin lesion. For larger or thicker lesions, a skin biopsy may be performed to rule out the presence of skin cancer. When to Seek Medical Attention: You should schedule an appointment with your healthcare provider if you notice persistent rough or scaly areas on sun-exposed skin. Treatment Options: Since approximately 5% of actinic keratoses may progress to squamous cell carcinoma, it is essential to have them evaluated and treated promptly. Treatment options include: Burning (electrical cautery): Using heat to destroy the lesion. Curettage and electrodesiccation: Scraping away the lesion and using electricity to eliminate any remaining abnormal cells. Excision: Surgically removing the lesion and closing the area with stitches. Cryotherapy: Freezing the lesion with liquid nitrogen to kill the cells. For individuals with multiple actinic keratoses, treatments that target larger areas and may cause temporary irritation and redness are often used. These include: Photodynamic therapy (PDT): A laser treatment that activates a photosensitizing agent to destroy abnormal cells. Chemical peels: Application of a chemical solution to remove the outer layers of skin. Topical creams: Medications such as 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) or imiquimod to treat the lesions. Prognosis: Actinic keratosis itself is benign and not harmful. However, about 5% of cases may progress to skin cancer, specifically squamous cell carcinoma. Removal of the lesions is typically effective in preventing progression. Possible Complications: Irritation and discomfort associated with the lesions. Scarring from treatment procedures. Development of squamous cell carcinoma. Prevention: To reduce the risk of actinic keratosis, it is crucial to minimize sun exposure and protect your skin. Recommendations include: Wearing protective clothing, such as wide-brimmed hats, long-sleeved shirts, long skirts, or pants. Avoiding sun exposure during midday hours when UV radiation is strongest. Using high-quality sunscreens with a sun protection factor (SPF) of at least 15. Choose sunscreens that block both UVA and UVB rays. Applying sunscreen before sun exposure and reapplying frequently, especially after swimming or sweating. Using sunscreen year-round, even during winter months. Avoiding sunlamps, tanning beds, and tanning salons. Additional Sun Safety Tips: Be aware that sun exposure is more intense near reflective surfaces like water, sand, concrete, or white-painted areas. UV radiation is stronger at the beginning of summer. Skin burns more quickly at higher altitudes.
